questions.explanation: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire in c. 321 BCE by overthrowing the Nanda dynasty with the help of his mentor Chanakya (Kautilya). Bindusara was his son; Ashoka was his grandson. Dasharatha was Ashoka's grandson (ruled after Ashoka's son Kunala). Chandragupta abdicated to become a Jain monk at Shravanabelagola.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Who was the Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya?
questions.explanation: Megasthenes (c. 350-290 BCE) was sent by Seleucus I Nicator to Chandragupta Maurya's court at Pataliputra. He wrote 'Indica' — a detailed account of Mauryan India (only fragments survive in quotations by later writers). Deimachus was a later ambassador sent to Bindusara. Dionysius was sent to an even later Mauryan court. Patrocles was a Seleucid explorer, not an ambassador to the Mauryas.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, economics, and military strategy, was written by:
questions.explanation: The Arthashastra is attributed to Kautilya (also known as Chanakya or Vishnugupta) — the legendary advisor of Chandragupta Maurya. It covers political theory, economics, diplomacy, war, administration, and espionage. Megasthenes wrote Indica. Panini was a Sanskrit grammarian (4th c. BCE) who wrote Ashtadhyayi. Patanjali is associated with the Yoga Sutras. The Arthashastra was rediscovered by R. Shamasastry in 1905.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Kalinga War, a turning point in Indian history, was fought by Ashoka in:
questions.explanation: The Kalinga War was fought c. 261 BCE — the 8th regnal year of Ashoka, who had been crowned c. 269 BCE. The massive casualties (per Ashoka's own Rock Edict XIII: '100,000 killed, 150,000 deported, many more died from secondary causes') led to his remorse and conversion to Buddhism. 232 BCE is Ashoka's approximate death year; 305 BCE was Chandragupta's war with Seleucus; 268 BCE is sometimes cited as Ashoka's coronation year.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Ashoka's edicts were written primarily in which script(s)?
questions.explanation: Ashoka's edicts (Rock, Pillar, Minor Rock, Minor Pillar, Cave) are primarily in Prakrit language using the BRAHMI script (across most of India — this is how the Ashokan edicts were deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837). The northwestern edicts (e.g., Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra) use the KHAROSTHI script. The Kandahar edict (bilingual Greek-Aramaic) uses GREEK and ARAMAIC — reflecting the Hellenistic populations of the frontier. Devanagari evolved much later (from Brahmi around the 7th c. CE).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Mauryan capital was located at:
questions.explanation: PATALIPUTRA (modern-day Patna, Bihar) was the capital of the Mauryan Empire — inherited from the preceding Nanda dynasty, which had itself inherited it from the Shishunaga dynasty. Megasthenes described Pataliputra as a huge walled city with 64 gates and 570 towers, 15 km long × 2.8 km wide. Ujjain, Taxila, Tosali, and Suvarnagiri were PROVINCIAL capitals under princes/governors. Kalinga (Dhauli/Jaugada region) was conquered by Ashoka.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which symbol on the Indian national flag is derived from Ashoka's Sarnath pillar?
questions.explanation: The ASHOKA CHAKRA — a navy-blue 24-spoke wheel — appears at the centre of the Indian tricolour. It is adapted from the 'Dharma Chakra' on the abacus of Ashoka's Sarnath Lion Capital. The Lion Capital itself (four lions back-to-back, on an abacus with four animals — lion, bull, horse, elephant — separated by smaller chakras) is India's State Emblem. Both symbols were adopted on 26 January 1950.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Mauryan administration was highly centralized. According to the Arthashastra, the state was divided into provinces, each under:
questions.explanation: Mauryan provinces were headed by princes of the royal family ('Kumaras' or 'Aryaputras') at the top four provincial capitals: Taxila (Uttarapatha), Ujjain (Avantirashtra), Tosali (Kalinga), Suvarnagiri (south). Other districts were headed by 'Pradesikas' (governors) with local officials like 'Rajukas' (revenue) and 'Yuktas' (secretariat). The king sat at Pataliputra with a Mantri Parishad (Council of Ministers) and a vast bureaucracy — a very centralised, non-republican polity.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Mauryan Empire declined and fragmented after the death of which ruler?
questions.explanation: After Ashoka's death (c. 232 BCE), the Mauryan Empire declined rapidly. His successors (Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan, Brihadratha) were weaker; administrative costs were huge; provincial governors rebelled. The LAST Mauryan, Brihadratha, was assassinated by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga c. 185 BCE, founding the Shunga dynasty. So Ashoka's death BEGAN the decline; Brihadratha's assassination ENDED the empire.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which of Ashoka's major rock edicts mentions the Kalinga War and his subsequent remorse?
questions.explanation: Major Rock Edict XIII is the most famous — it explicitly mentions the Kalinga War, the massive casualties, and Ashoka's remorse leading to adoption of Dhamma. The edict is NOT found at the Kalinga sites themselves (Dhauli, Jaugada — diplomatic avoidance). Other key edicts: Rock Edict I (ban on animal sacrifice), II (medical aid to humans and animals), VII (religious tolerance), XII (full religious tolerance to all sects).
